hops.afterHeading: Which protein? A screen, and the claim it refused to make
hops.title: A year of dead ends before Piezo1
hops.text: Bertrand Coste spent a year poking mouse Neuro2A cells with a glass probe while silencing candidate membrane-protein genes one at a time. Starting from roughly three hundred possible candidates, he worked through dozens with no luck: knock one down, poke the cell, and the current still fired. More than seventy candidates into the screen, silencing a little-studied gene called Fam38A finally made the poke-evoked current drop sharply. Ardem Patapoutian, who ran the lab, later recalled that Coste walked into his office very calmly and said, "I found it." They named the protein Piezo1, after the Greek word for pressure.

sources.citation: Ardem Patapoutian – Biographical, The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2021, NobelPrize.org
Scientific Background: Discoveries of Receptors for Temperature and Touch (Advanced Information), The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2021, NobelPrize.org

hops.afterHeading: Tension pays for area: from an energy to a curve
hops.title: How bacteria survive a rain shower
hops.text: When the salt outside a bacterium suddenly drops, as in a rain shower on salty soil, water floods in and the swelling cell stretches its membrane toward bursting. Escherichia coli relies mainly on two of seven stretch-gated channels. MscS activates at lower tension than MscL, which opens just short of cell rupture; in lab tests, cells lacking both fared much worse. In E. coli membrane patches, MscL reaches half activation near 10.4 mN/m, with an estimated in-plane area gain of about 20 nm² inferred from activation curves. At that tension, T × ΔA comes to roughly 50 k_BT, just enough to make open and closed equally likely.

hops.afterHeading: Reading a patch: from pressure to current, and back to an area
hops.title: The small bubble empties into the big one
hops.text: Join a small soap bubble to a big one through a tube, open the valve, and you might expect them to even out. They do not. The small bubble shrinks and blows its air into the big one until it is gone. For a soap film at fixed surface tension, the pressure inside rises as the radius shrinks, so the tight little sphere pushes harder. A patch under a pipette obeys the same geometry, read the other way round: the suction alone does not set the tension, because the dome's curvature changes it too. That is why Lewis and Grandl imaged every patch instead of trusting the pressure dial.

sources.citation: OpenStax College Physics 2e, Section 11.8: Cohesion and Adhesion in Liquids: Surface Tension and Capillary Action
